title: Transfer of Pain-related Expectations to Emotional Processing
summary:
The study investigates the extent to which expectations formed in a pain context transfer to the perception of emotional facial expressions.
Expectations will be induced through simulated brain–computer feedback.

Participants will be told that their individual pain sensitivity is being measured in the MRI scanner and fed back to them in real time. Light and dark orange cues will indicate low or high pain sensitivity, while a grey cue will mark the control condition without feedback. After the feedback, participants will either receive a brief heat stimulus on the skin or view a facial expression (neutral, fearful, happy). They will then rate either the intensity of the pain or the perceived positivity or negativity (valence) of the facial expression.

It is expected that pain-related expectations will influence the perception of emotional faces. Positive expectations will lead to more positive evaluations on the valence scale, whereas negative expectations will lead to more negative evaluations. These effects are expected to be accompanied by corresponding changes in activity within relevant brain regions.

interventions.name:
All three conditions (corresponding to Arm 1, Arm 2, and Arm 3) are presented to each participant in a pseudorandomized order in two variants: 1) in the domain of pain processing and then 2) in the domain of emotion processing.
Arms 1 to 3 last approximately 1 hour, comprising 30 trials in pain pro

Arm 2 – Nocebo condition:
A dark or light cue (counterbalanced across participants), combined with a mostly filled-out lightning bolt, is framed as the output of a BCI. It is used to induce the expectation of being in a pain-prone brain state.

Arm 3 –Control condition:
A grey visual cue signals the absence of BCI feedback, functioning as the control condition without directed expectation induction.

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
Age 18-35, Healthy
Exclusion criteria:
• Depressive symptoms (BDI score >= 14)
• Presence of acute or chronic somatic, neurological or psychiatric disorders
• Pregnancy
• Regular use of medication (except hormonal contraceptives)
• Use of illegal drugs, regular usage of psychotropic or analgesic substances
• Consumption of caffeine 2 hours before MRI testing and consumption of alcohol on the day of testing and the previous day
• Any impediments for MRI measurement (metal implants, non-removable piercings, heart pacemaker, tattoos close to the head, claustrophobia)
• Participation in a study involving deception within the past six months
